summary: This standards-track document defines a TRILL message to flush learned end-station address information. TRILL normally learns addresses by watching data traffic. A flush message lets an edge tell others to discard entries that may now be wrong.

eli5.summary: If someone moves house, the post office needs to throw away the old address. This message tells switches to forget addresses they have learned.

questions: what is the trill address flush message
how to clear learned mac addresses in trill
how do trill switches flush mac addresses
what are trill address flush tlv types
subtitle: A TRILL control message that lets one switch tell the others to forget learned MAC addresses.

tldr.problem: TRILL edge switches learn which switch each MAC address sits behind by watching traffic, and the built-in timeouts can be slow to clean up stale entries after a topology or configuration change.
tldr.mechanism: The Address Flush message is an RBridge Channel message that names the ingress nicknames, the VLANs or Fine-Grained Labels, and optionally the MAC addresses whose learned entries receivers should discard.
tldr.outcome: Switches can purge wrong entries explicitly and converge faster. The message is not authenticated by itself, so forged flushes can only cost efficiency, not misdeliver frames.

today: RFC 8383 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Flush Learned Addresses
sections.content:
By default, an edge TRILL switch (also called an RBridge) learns end-station MAC addresses from the data plane. It learns local addresses from native frames it receives, and remote addresses from the TRILL Data packets it decapsulates. All of this learning is scoped by a Data Label, which is a VLAN or a Fine-Grained Label (FGL).

TRILL already has ways to time out and clear that learning. The RFC says there are still cases where a switch should be able to explicitly ask remote RBridges to purge entries, to converge more rapidly. One example comes from a bridged LAN attached to the TRILL network through several RBridge ports. When one edge RBridge sees Spanning Tree topology change information, it can flush the MAC addresses for specific VLANs learned at the other edge RBridge ports.

A switch can easily flush its own local entries. This RFC defines the message used to ask others to flush entries learned from decapsulating TRILL Data packets.
sections.eli5: Normally switches forget old addresses slowly, like a note that fades over time. This message is a way to say 'erase that note right now'.

sections.title: How the Message Is Sent
sections.content:
The Address Flush message is an RBridge Channel protocol message. IANA assigned it Channel Protocol number 0x009, and the RBridge Channel Ethertype is 0x8946.

By default the message applies to addresses in the Data Label that follows the Inner Ethernet Addresses. It is usually sent as a multi-destination packet (TRILL Header M bit equal to one), so it reaches every TRILL switch offering end-station service in that VLAN or FGL. Both multi-destination and unicast flush messages SHOULD be sent at priority 6, because they are important control messages but less important than those that establish or maintain adjacency.

There are three variations. The Data Labels can be given explicitly, for cases where the message travels over a Management VLAN. The message can be unicast to clear one switch only. It can also be sent selectively to RBridges that have an access port in one of the listed VLANs or FGLs. Implementations should consider logging received flush messages, with protection against packet storms.
sections.eli5: The message usually goes to everyone in the neighborhood at once, like a loudspeaker announcement. It can also be a private note to one switch.

sections.title: The VLAN Block Format
sections.content:
The simple form is built for flushing by nickname and blocks of VLANs. After the RBridge Channel header it carries K-nicks, then that many 16-bit nicknames, then K-VLBs, then that many VLAN blocks.

  • K-nicks is the number of nicknames listed. If zero, the message applies only to the ingress nickname in the TRILL Header. If non-zero, it applies to the listed nicknames, and not to the ingress nickname unless it is listed too.
  • K-VLBs is the number of VLAN blocks. Zero means the extensible format of the next section. In this form it is at least one.
  • Each block has a Start.VLAN and an End.VLAN, 12 bits each, plus 4 reserved bits that MUST be sent as zero.

A block includes both ends, so a block of one VLAN has equal start and end. A start of 0x000 is treated as 0x001, and an end of 0xFFF is treated as 0xFFE. A block whose end is smaller than its start is ignored while the rest of the message is still processed. Blocks may overlap. The message flushes every address in an applicable VLAN that was learned from egressing TRILL Data packets whose ingress nickname applies. To flush all VLANs, use one block from 0x001 to 0xFFE.

Unknown or reserved nicknames in the list are ignored. If an incorrect nickname causes too much to be flushed, the network still works but is less efficient while entries are relearned.
sections.eli5: The simple message says 'forget what you learned from these switches, for these ranges of VLAN numbers'. A range is written as a start and an end.

sections.title: The Extensible TLV Format
sections.content:
When K-VLBs is zero, the rest of the message is a series of TLVs (type, length, value), each with an 8-bit type and an 8-bit length. This form handles FGLs, other VLAN encodings, and optionally specific MAC addresses. A receiver ignores TLVs of unknown or reserved types by skipping ahead with the Length byte. The same type may appear several times, and order does not matter.

Eight types are defined. VLANs can be given as blocks (type 1) or as a bit map (type 2). FGLs can be blocks (type 3), a list of 3-byte values (type 4) or a bit map (type 5). Type 6 means all Data Labels and must have Length zero. MAC addresses are given as a list (type 7) or as start and end blocks (type 8). Bit maps are most efficient for scattered values in a limited range, blocks for consecutive values, and lists for widely scattered single values.

A TLV whose length does not fit its type, for example a type 1 length that is not a multiple of 4, is corrupt and the whole message MUST be discarded. A length that runs past the payload makes the message corrupt and it MUST be ignored.

On requirements: every RBridge implementing Address Flush MUST implement types 1, 2 and 6. Those that can egress FGL packets MUST implement types 3, 4 and 5. Implementing types 7 and 8 is a SHOULD.
sections.eli5: The flexible message is like a form with optional boxes. You fill in only the boxes you need, and anyone who does not know a box just skips it.

sections.title: How a Receiver Decides What to Flush
sections.content:
A receiver parses all the TLVs and ends up with three sets, then flushes any learned entry that matches all three.

  • Data Labels: all of them if a type 6 TLV was seen. Otherwise the VLANs and FGLs accumulated from types 1 to 5. If none were accumulated, the set is empty and the message does nothing.
  • MAC addresses: all of them if the receiver does not implement types 7 and 8, or no addresses were accumulated. Otherwise the accumulated addresses. A receiver without MAC support therefore flushes every address in the named Data Labels, which is safe but may cause extra relearning.
  • Nicknames: the ingress nickname of the message if K-nicks is zero, otherwise the listed nicknames.

In a VLAN bit map or FGL bit map, a one bit means flush and a zero bit means leave alone. The numbers do not wrap around, and bits past the highest valid value are ignored.
sections.eli5: A switch reads the whole message, builds three lists (which networks, which devices, which switches), and erases only the notes that match all three.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigned 0x009 as the Address Flush protocol number in the RBridge Channel Protocols registry. It also created the TRILL Address Flush TLV Types registry as a subregistry, with registration procedure IETF Review. Its initial entries are types 0 and 255 (reserved), types 1 to 8 as above, and 9 to 254 unassigned.
sections.eli5: The numbers in the message are written in an official phone book so nobody else uses the same ones for something different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol itself provides no security assurances. Messages can be secured with the RBridge Channel Header Extension from RFC 7978, and it is RECOMMENDED that RBridges implementing Address Flush ignore messages that are not secured in a way that meets local security policy.

Without that, flush messages are fairly easy to forge. A forged message purges useful learned information that must be relearned, which is a denial-of-service attack on efficiency. The RFC states that it cannot cause a frame to be improperly delivered.
sections.eli5: If anyone can shout 'erase your notes', a prankster can make everyone redo work. They cannot make mail go to the wrong house, though.

fields.name: Start.VLAN
fields.desc: First VLAN ID in the block.

fields.name: End.VLAN
fields.desc: Last VLAN ID in the block.

items.label: Bit Map of VLANs
items.desc: Starting VLAN, then one bit per VLAN.

items.label: Bit Map of FGLs
items.desc: Starting FGL, then one bit per FGL.

items.label: All Data Labels
items.desc: Every VLAN and FGL; Length must be zero.
